findings.lesson_text: He is the son of Sycorax and the devil Setebos, born on the island.
findings.issue: Setebos is not Caliban's father. The lesson conflates the god Sycorax worshipped with the devil named as Caliban's father. In the play, Caliban calls Setebos 'my dam's god' (Act 1, Scene 2: 'His art is of such power / It would control my dam's god, Setebos, / And make a vassal of him') — Setebos is a deity Sycorax served, not Caliban's progenitor. Caliban's parentage comes from Prospero's insult: 'Thou poisonous slave, got by the devil himself / Upon thy wicked dam' (Act 1, Scene 2). The devil referenced there is unnamed; Setebos is an entirely different figure.
findings.canonical_truth: Caliban's mother is Sycorax. His father is described by Prospero as 'the devil himself' (Act 1, Scene 2: 'Thou poisonous slave, got by the devil himself / Upon thy wicked dam'). Setebos is the god that Sycorax worshipped, not Caliban's father. Students who memorise this lesson's version will give an incorrect character description.

findings.lesson_text: He holds his act of rescue over Ariel as a permanent debt: "Once in a month / Thou dost remember me what thou owest me."
findings.issue: This quotation does not appear in the play. The actual text of Act 1, Scene 2 is Prospero saying 'I must / Once in a month recount what thou hast been, / Which thou forget'st.' The lesson's invented version implies a recurring guilt-trip in which Ariel acknowledges a debt monthly; the canonical line has Prospero saying he is obliged to remind Ariel of her own history because Ariel forgets it. The direction of the obligation is reversed: in the text, Prospero does the reminding, not Ariel.
findings.canonical_truth: The canonical line (Act 1, Scene 2) is Prospero to Ariel: 'I must / Once in a month recount what thou hast been, / Which thou forget'st.' This means Prospero must periodically remind Ariel of her own past captivity under Sycorax — because Ariel tends to forget — not that Ariel periodically acknowledges owing Prospero a debt.

findings.lesson_text: "No sovereignty — / All things in common nature should produce / Without sweat or endeavour."
findings.issue: These two lines are presented as a single continuous quotation from Gonzalo, but they are separated in the text by two interruptions from Antonio and Sebastian. After 'No sovereignty —', Sebastian says 'Yet he would be king on't' and Antonio adds 'The latter end of his commonwealth forgets the beginning.' Only then does Gonzalo continue with 'All things in common nature should produce / Without sweat or endeavor.' The lesson gives a false impression of a single unbroken speech.
findings.canonical_truth: In Act 2, Scene 1, Gonzalo's speech 'No sovereignty—' is immediately interrupted by Sebastian ('Yet he would be king on't') and Antonio ('The latter end of his commonwealth forgets the beginning'). Gonzalo then continues 'All things in common nature should produce / Without sweat or endeavor.' The two halves of the quoted passage are separated by the mocking interjections that undercut Gonzalo's utopianism. Low severity because the words are Gonzalo's and the overall reading is sound, but students citing this as a single extended quotation will be citing a fabricated composite.
